title: Applying Science Learning PhET Simulation to Improve Process Skill and Knowledge Aspect of Junior High School Student
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using PhET simulation in science learning can improve junior high school students’ science process skills and knowledge about light and optical instruments. The authors frame the problem as students’ low engagement and weak learning outcomes in conventional science lessons, especially for abstract topics that are difficult to understand through text or lecture alone.

The intervention was a science lesson supported by the PhET simulation program, which the authors describe as functioning like a virtual laboratory. The study used a one-group pretest-posttest pre-experimental design with 30 eighth-grade students at SMPN 1 Ngoro, Indonesia. Data were collected through tests, observations, and student questionnaires; the paper reports pretest and posttest scores, N-gain, observed student activity, and student responses.

Results showed gains in both science process skills and knowledge, with high N-gain values reported for both outcomes. Student activity during learning was described as high, and student responses were largely positive. The authors conclude that PhET-assisted science learning can improve students’ process skills and knowledge aspects, while noting that careful preparation and time management are important for effective implementation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest study with no comparison group, so internal validity is limited. It is peer-reviewed, but the design provides only low-to-moderate credibility evidence for causal claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are large (N-gain 0.71 and 0.74) on a priority K-12 science topic, suggesting potentially meaningful impact. However, the lack of a control group and the small sample make the real-world impact uncertain.

interventions.use_case: PhET simulation-supported science learning for junior high school students on light and optical instruments, using virtual simulation as a classroom/virtual lab substitute to support inquiry and concept building.

finding.finding_summary: In a one-group pretest-posttest study with 30 grade-8 students, PhET-supported science learning increased science process skills from a pretest mean of 29 to a posttest mean of 80. The paper reports an N-gain of 0.71 (high criterion), with improvements across problem formulation, hypothesis formulation, data analysis, communication, and concluding.
finding.measure: Science process skills test / process skills assessment

finding.finding_summary: The same PhET intervention improved students' knowledge of light and optical instruments from a pretest mean of 24 to a posttest mean of 80 in the 30-student sample. The study reports an N-gain of 0.74 (high criterion), indicating substantial gains on cognitive knowledge indicators such as laws of reflection, image formation, and optical devices.
finding.measure: Knowledge test on light and optical instruments

finding.finding_summary: Student engagement/activity during PhET-based learning was described as high, with the highest observed activity being experiment/observation (18.3%) and low irrelevant behavior (3%). Students also reported a very positive response to the learning process (83%), with response items ranging from 77% to 90%.
finding.measure: Classroom activity observation and student response questionnaire
